definition: The gently sloping, submerged edge of a continent before the seabed drops into deep water.
A group or chain of islands.
Land that extends into water and stays joined to a larger landmass on one side.
A narrow strip of land joining two larger areas of land, with water on either side.
A narrow natural passage of water connecting two larger bodies of water.
A passage that water flows through, such as the waterway between two islands or the bed of a river.
A large arm of a sea or ocean partly enclosed by land.
A stretch of water where the shore curves inward. There is no strict size boundary between a bay and a gulf.
A narrow opening where water reaches into the land.
A shallow body of water partly cut off from a larger body of water by a reef, sandbank or barrier island.
The tidal stretch at a river mouth where river water meets the sea.
A steep-sided valley carved by a glacier and later flooded by the sea.
A ring or partial ring of coral reef around a lagoon, sometimes with low islands on the reef.
A ridge of rock or coral rising close to the water surface.
A coral reef running offshore with a lagoon between the reef and the coast.
Land that projects from a coast into the water, often as a rocky point.
A narrow ridge of sand or gravel built by currents, attached to land at one end.
A mountain rising from the ocean floor whose summit stays underwater.
A long, narrow, exceptionally deep depression in the ocean floor.
The strip of shore covered at high tide and exposed at low tide.
Low, nearly level mud or sand that the tide regularly covers and exposes.
The steeper submerged slope connecting a continent’s shallow shelf to the deep ocean.
The rise of deeper water towards the surface, often bringing nutrients up with it.
The amount of dissolved salt in water.
Describes water saltier than fresh water but less salty than typical seawater.
Waves that have travelled away from the winds that generated them.
A stream or river that flows into a larger stream or river.
A channel that branches from a river and takes water away from its main course.
The place where streams or rivers meet.
The streams and source areas where a river begins.
The area of land from which water drains to a particular outlet, such as a river mouth or a lake.
High ground separating areas whose surface water drains to different outlets.
Land built from sediment that a river deposits as it enters a lake or sea.
Relatively flat land beside a river that the river can cover during floods.
A winding bend in a stream or river.
A curved lake left behind when a river cuts off one of its bends.
Water from rain or melting snow that flows over land into streams and lakes.
The volume of water flowing past a point in a river per unit of time.
Loose material such as sand, silt or clay that water, wind or ice can carry and deposit.
Tiny mineral grains finer than sand but coarser than clay.
A body of water stored for later use, often a lake formed by damming a river.
A layer of rock or loose material that stores groundwater and lets it flow through.
Water beneath the land surface in saturated rock, sand or soil.
A place where groundwater flows naturally out onto the surface.
A valley or streambed in a dry region that usually carries water only after rain.
Flat ground coated in salts left behind as shallow water evaporates.
A drainage basin whose water has no surface route to the ocean.
The upper surface of the ground zone where pores and cracks are filled with water.
A stretch of river where a steep or rocky bed makes the water fast and turbulent.
A broad area of relatively level land raised above the surrounding country.
A long, steep slope separating two areas of land at different heights.
A narrow, deep valley with steep sides, often cut by a river.
A small, steep-sided valley, usually cut by running water.
A long, narrow crest of high ground.
A hollow or low-lying area surrounded by higher ground.
The wearing away and removal of material by water, wind or ice.
The breakdown of rock in place by chemical reactions or physical forces.
The settling or accumulation of material carried by water, wind or ice.
A mound or ridge of loose sand built by wind or flowing water.
A mass of ice formed from accumulated snow that moves under its own weight.
A ridge or accumulation of rock and sediment deposited by a glacier.
A smooth, elongated hill shaped beneath moving ice, often occurring in groups.
Terrain where dissolving rock, usually limestone, creates caves, sinkholes and underground streams.
A hollow that forms when material dissolves underground or the ground collapses into a cavity.
A mineral deposit that grows down from a cave ceiling.
A mineral deposit that grows up from a cave floor.
A rock made mainly of calcium carbonate, often from shells or other marine remains.
Rock made of sand grains compacted and cemented together.
A dark, fine-grained rock formed when relatively fluid lava cools.
A coarse-grained rock whose visible crystals grew as molten rock cooled slowly underground.
A moving slab of Earth’s rigid outer layer that can carry continents, ocean floor or both.
A long zone where Earth’s crust is being pulled apart.
A break in Earth’s crust along which the rock on either side has moved.
Molten or partly molten rock beneath Earth’s surface.
Molten rock that has reached Earth’s surface, or the rock formed when it cools.
A large volcanic hollow formed mainly when the ground collapses above a partly emptied magma reservoir.
A bowl-shaped hollow, often made by a volcanic eruption or an impact from space.
A tunnel left when the surface of a lava flow hardens and the molten rock inside drains away.
Describes heat from inside Earth, as in the water of a hot spring.
Describes a climate with so little available moisture that most plants struggle to grow.
A broad ecological region recognised by its climate and characteristic vegetation or other living communities.
Tropical or subtropical grassland with scattered trees and a marked dry season.
A broad, mostly treeless grassland in a comparatively dry climate.
A cold, mostly treeless biome where the growing season is short and plants grow low to the ground.
Forest sustained by abundant rainfall, found in both tropical and temperate climates.
Mountain forest often immersed in low cloud, where vegetation collects moisture from the mist.
Land flooded or soaked often enough to support plants and soils adapted to wet conditions.
A wetland dominated by soft-stemmed plants such as reeds, grasses and sedges.
A wetland dominated by trees or shrubs.
A peat-forming wetland fed mainly by rain or snow, usually acidic and low in nutrients.
Partly decayed plant material that builds up where the ground stays so wet that decay is slow.
A salt-tolerant tree or shrub that grows on tropical or subtropical tidal shores.
A seasonal shift in prevailing winds, often bringing a marked change between wet and dry weather.
A relatively dry area on the sheltered side of mountains, after rising air has lost moisture on the other side.
Describes the climate zones between the tropics and the polar regions, often with distinct seasons.
Describes a species that occurs naturally only in a particular area.
Ground that stays at or below freezing for at least two consecutive years.
Describes a country without a coastline on the open ocean or on a sea connected to it.
Describes a landlocked country whose neighbours are all landlocked too.
A territory completely surrounded by the territory of one other country or region.
A part of a territory separated from its main part by other territory. Some exclaves are also enclaves.
A point where three territorial boundaries meet.
An imaginary line running from pole to pole along one longitude.
Angular distance north or south of the equator, measured in degrees.
Angular distance east or west of the prime meridian, measured in degrees.
The imaginary circle at zero degrees latitude, halfway between the poles.
One half of Earth, such as the half north of the equator.
A seasonal lake in limestone country that fills and drains as groundwater rises and falls.
Land where a layer of peat has accumulated over time.
The fine-leaved shrubland of South Africa’s Cape region, where many plants depend on periodic fires.
Open grassland or scrub country in southern Africa.
A place in a dry region where a local water supply supports vegetation.
The upper layer of a rainforest formed by the crowns of its trees.
In geology, a sheet of once-molten rock that cuts across older rock layers.
Remains or traces of a once-living organism preserved from the geological past.
The measurement and mapping of depth and shape beneath a body of water.
One of the vast, connected bodies of salt water covering most of Earth.
A named body of salt water, often partly enclosed by land and connected to an ocean. Some large inland lakes also carry this name.
A broad coastal waterway, often between an island and the mainland, or a large inlet from the sea.
A sustained flow of seawater in a particular direction.
A body of standing inland water, fresh or salty, occupying a basin.
A natural stream of water that flows along a channel toward another river, a lake, the sea, or an inland basin.
A region with very little precipitation. Deserts can be hot or cold.
A biome where grasses dominate and trees are sparse.
The broad belt of cold northern forest dominated by coniferous trees.
Relating to the belt of Earth between the Tropics of Cancer and Capricorn.
Relating to the high latitudes around the North or South Pole.
